gen.process_notes:
Write mode. I read SKILL.md, tells.md (all of it) and personal-essay.md (all of it, with extra attention to sections 4, 5 and 10), and I skimmed examples.md.

Plan:
- Spine: the hard C in "Carvalho", which is both the shop's name and her own last name. Arc: "Hi, shoe repair" at the start, then three tries at "Carvalho Shoe Service" last month, with the man waiting. The essay moves from the phone, to the shop and her heel-reading, to Avó (who calls her Lurdes and can't say her name yet but can say "sapato"), to aphasia and speech therapy, and back to the phone.
- Reflections all use the student's own words: "It's funny, because she's relearning the words and I'm learning them for the first time"; "I kind of wanted them to be connected, and they're not"; "I don't fully believe her yet"; "I haven't figured out whether that was a yes or a no."
- Left out, about 30% of the interview by word count: the whole AP Chem lie / forged signature / kitchen table / 212-item lie list story (the biggest chunk, and a separate spine better kept for a supplement), plus Science Olympiad, Portuguese Club treasurer, the GPA and the 5K time.

Audit fixes:
- Kept only two kicker endings ("I don't fully believe her yet." and "which we don't."). The tells file names "She can't say my name yet" and "We don't." as observed kickers, so the sapato line sits mid-paragraph and "we don't" is folded into a clause.
- Avoided the staged self-correction the notes invite ("never once... actually last month") and stated it directly: "I had never once... until last month."
- Cut seven "which" clauses down to two.
- Removed "What I'm best at," because it echoed the interview question "weirdly good at," and removed "for a long time," which the notes don't support.
- No em dashes, no words from the tell lists, no stated lessons.

Fact diff: every claim checked against the notes. Corrections:
- Removed "in Fall River" for the shop. Only the student's hometown is given; the shop's city is not.
- Fixed a doubled "drives".

Small additions that are not in the notes:
- Glosses of general-knowledge terms: what "supinate" means, and "sapato" = shoe.
- The observation that "Hi, shoe repair" has no C in it.
- Inferences the notes support: "waited through the first two" (from "third try, the guy waited"), "someday", "back in middle school", "what I was doing".

Length: the spine material, with a third left out, gave about 520 words. I reached 551 with clarifying phrasing rather than new content or invented detail. That puts it at the bottom of the 550-650 target. No title line and no sample label in the text.

judged.reasons:
Y is the better essay for an admissions reader, mostly because it has a real shape. It sets up the problem early: "What I could not do, for years, was answer the phone." Then it gets to the payoff, "But I said our name, and he heard it," and closes on a callback that earns its place: "She can't say my name yet... My avó is still working on mine. I'll wait for her, too." That ending ties the stutter, the family name and the grandmother into one point, which is the "so what" this prompt asks for. The trouble is the joints between sections. They are stock essay connectors that a strict editor would flag as AI tells: "The shop taught me a different kind of listening," "People tell you a lot without saying a word, if you know where to look," "That mattered more than I expected." The heel-reading section doesn't actually connect to the aphasia section, so "That mattered more than I expected" is a link the essay asserts but never shows. The climax is overwritten: "the word that belonged to me came out of my own mouth instead of being traded for a safer one." Y also invents things beyond the notes. It makes up where her interest came from ("Sitting across from her, I started wondering how the brain gets words back") and adds motives she never stated ("as if my grandmother's struggle and mine were one problem"). It also gets a fact slightly wrong: she did answer the phone, just with "Hi, shoe repair," so "could not... answer the phone" overstates it. And the man waited through the first two tries, not "all of them." Its diction is more polished and adult than hers ("completely different" and "far more" where she said "totally different" and "way more"). It also leaves out the dad's thumb and the dad's "The shop isn't a person" line.

X sounds more like a real person. It opens plainly ("I hate the phone."), keeps her phrasing ("I kind of wanted them to be connected, and they're not," "way more than her left," "smell like a cowboy's basement"), and uses almost no stock transitions. It is also more specific and more faithful to the notes: "which has no C in it," "My dad, whose right thumb is stained black from the dye," and the dad's exact quote. The cost is that it reads like the interview answers re-paragraphed, mostly in the order she gave them. Paragraph 2 is a list of skills ("I mostly do the counter and the tickets... I can resole a sneaker in 25 minutes. I can also tell how someone walks..."). The supination gloss reads like a textbook: "(when they walk, their weight rolls onto the outside of the foot)." X never says what any of this means. The parallel between her family name and her grandmother not being able to say "my name" is left for the reader to find. And the ending is deadpan to the point of fizzling: "He was calling to ask if we fix purses, which we don't." That restraint is human and has some charm, but it gives up the insight the prompt is looking for.

Net verdict: Y wins on craft and arc despite its tells and invented connections. X wins on human-likeness, voice, specificity and accuracy to the notes.

judged.reasons:
X is the better personal statement because it has a shape. It sets up a problem ("What I could not do, for years, was answer the phone"), pays it off with the three-try phone call ("He wanted to know if we fix purses. We don't. But I said our name, and he heard it"), and closes with a mirror image that gives the essay its point: "She can't say my name yet... My avó is still working on mine. I'll wait for her, too." The man who waits for her and the granddaughter who waits for Rosa make a real "so what": patience with broken speech, given and received. The cost is that X uses the moves of a polished college essay, the ones an experienced reader learns to spot. It has a one-line dramatic paragraph, thesis-style bridges ("The shop taught me a different kind of listening", "That mattered more than I expected", "People tell you a lot without saying a word, if you know where to look"), and an over-written beat ("the word that belonged to me came out of my own mouth instead of being traded for a safer one"). It also invents things: a resolve ("But I want to find out if she's right"), a cause for her interest in the field ("Sitting across from her, I started wondering..."), and a small factual stretch, since she did answer the phone, just not with the name, and "for years" is never stated.

Y keeps very close to the facts. Its only outside addition is the parenthetical definition of supination. Its voice sounds like a real 17-year-old: it opens with the blunt "I hate the phone", and the hedges come straight from her ("I kind of wanted them to be connected, and they're not"). The deadpan ending, "He was calling to ask if we fix purses, which we don't", avoids the neat bow. That restraint and the plain sentences make it read as more human. As writing for this prompt, though, it is mostly a list of facts in a new order. Paragraph two lists one detail after another ("I mostly do the counter and the tickets... I can resole a sneaker in 25 minutes. I can also tell how someone walks"). Details get forced into sentences, as in "My dad, whose right thumb is stained black from the dye, noticed". The last paragraph puts two unrelated beats side by side, the dad's "The shop isn't a person, it doesn't need anyone" and the phone call, with nothing connecting them. Y never says what any of this means: the stutter, the aphasia, sapato and the unspoken name sit next to each other, but the essay never brings them together. It also over-explains in places ("which has no C in it"). An admissions officer would enjoy the details in Y and still finish without an insight. X makes the reader feel something, at the price of a few lines that sound produced.

gen.process_notes:
I read SKILL.md, references/tells.md and references/personal-essay.md (sections 4, 5 and 10), plus examples.md. I worked in Write mode, using the case for a sample essay about a fictional person.

PLAN
- Spine: getting words out, or not. Her stutter blocks "Carvalho" on the shop phone. Her grandmother Rosa has aphasia and can't say Ines's name. Ines lied about a 54, then had to explain the whole test in Portuguese without the word for "mole." She wants to study how the brain gets words back. The turn comes at the end, when she says the name on the third try.
- Arc: the "Hi, shoe repair" habit plus the shop and her stutter; then Rosa, placed right after the stutter so the reader sees the two side by side; then the AP Chem lie and her lie list (highest stakes, being wrong, linked to Rosa through Portuguese words); then her finding that stuttering and aphasia are "totally different things," her study plans and Ms. Halvorsen; then the phone call, which calls back to the opening. This breaks the interview's order on purpose: Rosa comes before AP Chem, and the "small things" phone call becomes the ending.
- Left out: the heel anecdote about the woman who drives for work, the 61-entry count, the dad quote "the shop isn't a person" and its yes-or-no reflection (cut so the essay doesn't end three paragraphs on open doubts), the dye-stained thumb, Science Olympiad, Portuguese Club, the 3.9 GPA and cross-country 24:40. The heel skill and the notebook (entry 1 is dad's boots) survive as one sentence. The dad quote and the heel anecdote could go in a supplement.
- Reflection lines, all in her own words and each placed after the scene that earns it: "which was really bad"; "I'm still not sure if the list makes me more honest or just better at noticing" (after the lie list); "It's funny, because she's relearning the words and I'm learning them for the first time" (after the flashcards); "I kind of wanted them to be connected, and they're not"; "I don't fully believe her yet." I added no reflections, motives or causes of my own. The essay never says why she finally said the name, or why she stopped correcting Rosa, because the notes don't say.

AUDIT
- Content: every sentence is specific and nothing echoes the prompt.
- Staging: the one "wanted X, it's not" line is a belief she really held, so it stays. No importance flags and no -ing tails.
- Inflation and lessons: none, and no "taught me."
- Rhythm: sentence lengths run from 4 to 31 words, and paragraphs from 43 to 172 words.
- Endings: two kicker-style endings ("I don't fully believe her yet"; "...which we don't," which I folded into the sentence before it rather than leaving it to stand alone as "We don't."). The other paragraphs end on content or on her longer reflection. I moved "She can't say my name yet" mid-paragraph so it doesn't end one, and I avoided the staged self-correction about the phone.
- Words and format: I scanned for the listed tell words (none) and checked for em or en dashes (0). I used parentheses, semicolons and a colon. No title.

FACT DIFF
Every name, number, date and quote is in the notes: Pleasant Street, 1994, Barge cement, "cowboy's basement," 25 minutes, entry 1 dad's boots, "Hi, shoe repair," about a year, 54 and 85, three weeks, Mr. Oduya, two hours, "the unit thing, like a dozen," B+, 212 items, October of sophomore year, "I'm almost there," Rosa, two years ago, Lurdes, Tuesdays and Thursdays, agulha and telemovel, Ms. Halvorsen, last month, third try, purses. The only addition is the gloss "sapato (shoe)," a plain translation that matches the notes' own glosses.

Final length is 559 words, inside the 550-650 target and under the 650 Common App limit.

"Between her flashcards and that patient caller, I've learned that the most useful thing a listener can do is wait." (the notes never say she waits for her avó; the lesson is made up)
"My best skill there requires no talking." (framing that is not in the notes, and it clashes with "I said out loud" two sentences later)
"on Pleasant Street in Fall River" (the notes place the student in Fall River and the shop on Pleasant Street; they never say the shop is in Fall River)
"until last month I couldn't say our family's name to a stranger on the phone" (the notes say she never did, not that she couldn't)
"worst on hard sounds like 'C'" / "I read about aphasia all the time now" (small step-ups from "especially" and "a lot")
judged.reasons:
X is the better essay because it has a shape. It opens with "Until last month, I answered the phone at my dad's shop by saying, 'Hi, shoe repair,'" and comes back to the shop phone at the end. Each section hands off to the next with a real hinge. "I keep another list, on my phone, and I'm less proud of why" moves from the heel notebook to the lie list. "Noticing is most of what I do on Tuesdays and Thursdays" turns her line "better at noticing" into the avó section. The avó paragraph closes on "She can say 'sapato.' Shoe.", which quietly ties the grandmother to the shoe shop. X also keeps the best concrete material: the supination detail, the driver's worn right heel and "61 entries."

X has three weaknesses. First, the last paragraph explains itself too much. "My avó and I are both working on names" and "I've learned that the most useful thing a listener can do is wait. I'd like to make a career of it" read like the tidy moral counselors (and AI) tack on. That waiting lesson is also invented, since the notes never show her waiting for Rosa. Second, "My best skill there requires no talking" is contradicted by "I said out loud" two sentences later. Third, the file is 651 words including the title, which would break the 650 limit if the title is pasted in.

Y is accurate. I found no unsupported claims, and it stays under the limit at 559 words. But it is mostly the notes reordered, often word for word: "which was really bad", "which I'm not good at for chemistry words", "she laughed at that part." That keeps a real teen voice, but it also keeps the clumsy phrasing. The first paragraph crams in the hoodie smell, the counter, the finishing machine, "I can resole a sneaker in 25 minutes" and the heel notebook in a single breath before "But I hate the phone." Its best material, reading how people walk, gets one passing clause and loses the driver story entirely. There are no transitions: the avó, the AP Chem lie, the career plans and the phone call sit in separate blocks. The lie-list paragraph has no link to anything around it.

Y's ending, "He was calling to ask if we fix purses, which we don't," is pleasantly understated. It also never links the stutter, Rosa's aphasia and the speech-pathology goal, so the reader has to find the point alone. Y reads like a real student's competent rough draft and has fewer AI tells than X's ending. X reads more like a skilled writer's work, even though it is over-polished in places.

judged.reasons:
X is the interview notes put back into paragraphs. Each paragraph is one interview answer with the question removed, and nothing connects them. Paragraph 1 starts with the phone hook ("I used to answer the phone ... with 'Hi, shoe repair.'"), then drifts through the smell, the machine, "I can resole a sneaker in 25 minutes" and the heel notebook. Only after that does it come back with "But I hate the phone." That puts "My dad noticed what I was doing" a long way from what he noticed. The next paragraphs start cold: "My avó, Rosa, had a stroke two years ago...", "Sophomore year I got a 54...", "I read a lot about aphasia now." X also loses the best details. It gives the skill only in general terms ("From the wear on someone's heels I can tell how they walk"). It drops the driver whose right heel rested by the pedal, the supination detail and the 61 entries. Many phrases are copied word for word from the notes ("which was really bad", "totally different things; I kind of wanted them to be connected"). That gives a real teen voice, but it reads like a transcript, not like a writer who chose what to say. The ending, "He was calling to ask if we fix purses, which we don't.", is a quiet callback. Still, X never says why any of this matters, so the avó and lie-list sections seem to come from separate essays.

Y is built as one story. The title and first line ("Until last month, I answered the phone ... 'Hi, shoe repair.'") set up a frame that pays off later. Y also uses transitions that do real work. "My best skill there requires no talking" connects the stutter to the heel-reading. "I keep another list, on my phone, and I'm less proud of why" moves from the heel notebook to the lie list. "Noticing is most of what I do on Tuesdays and Thursdays" picks up the lie list's "better at noticing" and leads to the grandmother. Y keeps the strongest specifics (the supination detail, the driver, "61 entries", Fall River). Its short, dry lines sound like a person with a sense of humor: "She can say 'sapato.' Shoe." and "We don't."

Y's weak spot is the last paragraph. "Between her flashcards and that patient caller, I've learned that the most useful thing a listener can do is wait. I'd like to make a career of it." spells out the connection with a neat moral, which an AI-wary reader will notice. It is also an invented insight. Still, it gives the essay a real point that ties together the stutter, the aphasia and speech-language pathology ("My avó and I are both working on names" is earned). X has no such point.

Y takes a few small liberties with the facts. The driving becomes her deduction, the parent signature becomes "her signature", and "couldn't say our family's name" overstates what the notes say. It also sits right at the limit: 651 words with the title. X sticks closer to the facts, but it reads like a reformatted interview, not a skilled writer's essay. Y is clearly the better essay. It also reads more like a skilled human's work, though by less, because its tidy closing moral is its most machine-like moment.

audit.verdict: This is concrete, specific writing with no vocabulary, em-dash or corrective-framing tells. What gives it away is the structure: every paragraph ends on a wry or poignant kicker, short negative tags ('now I don't', 'which we don't') keep recurring, and the topics sit one per paragraph inside a bookend arc. That is the pattern an anti-AI rewrite leaves behind. Cut the kickers down to one or two and fold in the orphan details.

Neither essay invents statistics, studies or named sources. Both take a clear full-day-ban position and answer the same two objections: learning to manage phones, and parent emergencies. Both even reuse the same idea about how families reached students before cell phones. The differences come down to specificity, voice and how honestly each handles the hardest objection.

Y is more concrete and reads more like a real student wrote it. It builds its points from small scenes: a phone that "buzzes against a desk during a quiz, or lights up inside an open backpack, and half the class turns to look". Teachers who disagree: "One lets students use their phones as calculators; the next takes a phone the moment she sees it". A lunch table that becomes "a row of people reading separate screens". And the hallway video, where "the person in the video has to sit through fifth period knowing who has seen it." Its answer to the self-management objection is the stronger of the two. It explains why the test is unfair ("Asking a sixteen-year-old to resist that for an entire school day, while also following a chemistry lecture, sets students up to fail and then punishes them for failing") rather than just pointing to evenings and weekends. It is also the only essay that faces the lockdown case directly: "A student hiding in a dark classroom would want to text home... I don't think a ban fully answers this." It turns that admission into a condition the policy has to meet: "A school that can't make that promise isn't ready to collect phones yet." The contractions, the "we", and "students will hate that part most" give it a student's voice. Its weaknesses: there is no real concluding paragraph, so the essay stops on the emergency objection. The attention paragraph is thin and repeats the intro. And "A phone in a locker can't buzz" is sloppy.

X has the better single idea and the cleaner arc. The point about a group chat being a shared problem is genuinely clever: "A student who turns her phone off on her own misses the plans and the jokes... When every phone in the building is off, the chat pauses for everyone and nobody falls behind." So is "Looking takes a second, but wondering lasts the whole class." Its closing line works: "a text sent during second period reads the same after the last bell, and the lesson taught in second period happens only once." However, X's prose is more formal and more visibly built from balanced contrasts. Lines like "The second is not where the time goes." and "That keeps the problem alive." are short, tidy declaratives, and it avoids contractions throughout ("I do not know whether..."). Together these make it feel more polished than lived-in. Its examples are thinner: the group chat, "who is picking whom up after practice", calculators and whiteboard photos. Its emergency rebuttal skips the hard case. It says a student "can get to one in seconds", which quietly weakens its own "off and zipped away" rule and never mentions lockdowns.
